newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hong Kong smuggling checks irk oil traders.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong smuggling checks irk oil traders.

text.p: Asian oil traders said on Wednesday they feared heightened harbour customs checks by the new authorities in Hong Kong to prevent diesel smuggling into China could hamper their legitimate business.
Oil traders said the freer flow of information on imports and exports between China and the Special Administrative Region (SAR) would help authorities crack down on smuggling more effectively.

"Because of easier cross checks by both the Chinese and Hong Kong authorities on oil smuggling after the handover, and with more than half of (diesel) imports into China illegal, trade from Hong Kong could come to a standstill," said a source at state-owned China Resources Company (CRC).
"Customs on both sides could now exchange notes to tally figures on exports and imports figures," the CRC source said.
China's anti-smuggling campaign began as early as April, ahead of the July 1 handover of Hong Kong.
It intensified policing of routes between Hong Kong and China and nabbed smugglers who tried to avoid paying the $60-per-tonne taxes for diesel entering the mainland.
Each month, Hong Kong exports to China about 200,000 tonnes of oil products, mostly diesel, on a legitimate basis.
In addition, a lot of diesel sold into Hong Kong is later smuggled into China.
Chinese state media has reported that about one million tonnes of diesel have been smuggled into China so far this year.
Traders say the actual amount is much higher, with one estimating as much as 1.5 million tonnes of diesel smuggled each month during the first half of this year.
The crackdown against smuggling has affected legitimate exports of diesel from Hong Kong to China as the process of intensive checks slows down ship movements.
It also discourages genuine buyers in China who fear delays in deliveries of their products that give them higher demurrage costs, traders said.
Since the curbs hamper oil products movement into southern China from Hong Kong, it has hit the profits of oil companies in the territory, traders said.
Smugglers find the illicit activity lucrative and have shifted their illicit trade from traditional hot spots in southern Guandong to Fujian, Hainan and Guanxi provinces.
This in turn has prompted the Chinese authorities to extend their checks to other areas.
"Sellers in Hong Kong would sell their oil regardless who the buyers may be so long as they are able to pay for the oil," said a trader with a major oil company.
"But the buyers may decide to go around customs officials and evade paying duties and taxes in southern ports of China."
Oil traders in Hong Kong said that while such illicit trade should be eliminated, they noted that the territory was a major point of entry into China for oil products.
As most exporters sell their oil, mainly diesel, on a free-on-board Hong Kong basis, any clampdown on smuggling would significantly reduce exports to China, they added.
Exporters in Hong Kong said they were concerned that Chinese buyers might look elsewhere for cheaper oil because they had to pay higher values for the legitimate imports.
"End-users in China may look to Okinawa, South Korea Singapore, Taiwan to import directly," said the CRC source.
